channel.title: Distributed Systems Handbook
channel.description: New and rewritten pages of the Distributed Systems Handbook.

item.title: Multi-Leader Replication: Write Conflicts and Resolution
item.description: How several leaders accept writes and replicate to each other, why concurrent writes conflict, and how detection and resolution must converge in production.

item.title: Replication Lag Problems: Read-Your-Own-Writes
item.description: Why reads from lagging followers break read-your-writes, monotonic and prefix order, and how time windows, LSN/GTID tokens and waits restore them.

item.title: Failover and Leader Election: The Split-Brain Risk
item.description: How a replicated database detects a failed leader, elects one successor without losing acknowledged writes, and fences the old one, with real tools.

item.title: Leader-Based Replication: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous
item.description: How a leader ships an ordered change log to followers, what async, semi-sync and sync acks guarantee, and how PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB do it.

item.title: Data Partitioning / Sharding
item.description: How a dataset too large for one node is split so each key has one owner, why placement trades locality for load spread, and how to read this chapter.

item.title: Secondary Indexes in Partitioned Data: Local vs. Global
item.description: How secondary indexes work in partitioned stores: local indexes that scatter reads, global ones that fan out writes, how each stays correct, and failures.

item.title: Colocated Joins: Placing Related Data on the Same Shard
item.description: How one placement key for related tables makes distributed joins and transactions local, how Citus, Vitess and Spanner do it, and how colocation fails.

item.title: Dynamic Rebalancing: Zero-Downtime Strategies
item.description: How partitioned stores move data between nodes under live traffic: copy, catch-up and fenced cutover, with Kafka, MongoDB and Vitess, and how moves fail.

item.title: Consistent Hashing and Virtual Nodes (vnodes)
item.description: How a hash ring moves only a minimal share of keys on membership change, why virtual nodes fix skew, and how vnode count trades balance for repair cost.

item.title: Skew and Hot-Spot Problems: Real-World Scenarios
item.description: Why a partitioned system is limited by its hottest partition, where skew comes from, how to find heavy keys, and which techniques remove hot spots.

item.title: Hash Partitioning: Uniform Distribution
item.description: How hash partitioning maps keys via modulo, fixed slots or hash ranges, how uniform the result really is, and how mismatched hashes and resizing break it.

item.title: Key-Range Partitioning: Advantages and Range Scans
item.description: How range-partitioned stores split sorted keys, route and split ranges under live traffic, and why the order that makes scans cheap creates hot spots.

item.title: Communication Protocols & API Design
item.description: How services exchange requests and events over an unreliable network, and how this part's chapters on calls, messaging, contracts and balancing fit.

item.title: Load Balancing
item.description: How interchangeable replicas are made to act as one service, why each balancing decision trades information quality for cost, and how to read this chapter.

item.title: Health-Aware Routing and Connection Draining
item.description: How load balancers combine health checks with outlier detection, why ejection caps and panic thresholds matter, and how to drain a backend cleanly.

item.title: Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) and Anycast
item.description: How DNS-based global load balancing and BGP anycast steer users across regions, how fast each reacts to failure, and why production edges combine the two.

item.title: Client-Side vs. Server-Side Load Balancing
item.description: Whether load balancing runs in a proxy tier or inside every client, and how that choice shapes discovery, failure detection and connection counts.

item.title: Algorithms: Round Robin, Least Connections, Weighted, Consistent Hashing
item.description: How round robin, least connections, weighted and hash-based balancing pick a backend, what each actually equalizes, and how each fails in production.

item.title: L4 vs. L7 Load Balancing: Transport vs. Application Layer
item.description: How layer 4 balancers pin flows from packet headers, how layer 7 proxies terminate and re-issue each request, and what each costs in CPU and failures.

item.title: API Gateway and Service Contracts
item.description: How request-response APIs are exposed safely across teams, why edge policies are cheap but not authoritative, and how to read this chapter's six topics.

item.title: Throttling and Rate Limiting at the Gateway Level
item.description: How API gateways enforce per-caller rate limits across many instances: local vs. global counters, the 429 contract, product differences, and failures.

item.title: Idempotency and Safe HTTP Methods
item.description: What safe and idempotent HTTP methods allow, how idempotency keys make POST retries safe, and how lease expiry and replica reads bring duplicates back.

item.title: Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (Pact)
item.description: How consumer-driven contracts with Pact capture real consumer expectations, verify them against providers, and become a deployment gate, plus how they fail.

item.title: OpenAPI / Swagger: Contract-First Development
item.description: How OpenAPI models an HTTP API, how a contract-first pipeline lints, diffs, mocks and validates it, and what that pipeline cannot prove in production.

item.title: Backend for Frontend (BFF) Pattern
item.description: How a Backend for Frontend composes data for one client, why it must stay free of domain rules, and how its fan-out latency and failures add up.

item.title: API Gateway Pattern: Single Entry Point, Routing, Auth
item.description: How an API gateway routes and authenticates requests at the edge, which invariants keep edge authentication sound, and how a shared entry layer fails.

item.title: Asynchronous Messaging Fundamentals
item.description: Why a durable broker trades immediate, visible failure for delayed, invisible failure, and how to read this chapter's eight messaging topics.

item.title: Dead Letter Queues and Poison Message Handling
item.description: How consumers tell poison messages from transient failures, how bounded retries and dead-letter queues prevent stalls, and how to redrive a DLQ safely.

item.title: Schema Evolution and Schema Registry: Avro, Protobuf, and Compatibility Modes
item.description: How message schemas evolve without breaking readers, what each compatibility mode guarantees, and how Avro, Protobuf and a schema registry enforce it.

item.title: AsyncAPI: Documenting Asynchronous Contracts
item.description: How an AsyncAPI document describes an application's channels and messages, what it can guarantee across independent services, and how to keep it accurate.

item.title: At-Least-Once, At-Most-Once, and Exactly-Once Semantics
item.description: Why lost messages and lost acks force a choice between loss and duplicates, and how deduplication turns at-least-once delivery into exactly-once effects.

item.title: RabbitMQ: Exchange Types and Routing
item.description: How RabbitMQ routes messages through exchanges and bindings, how each exchange type matches, and what happens to unroutable messages.

item.title: Pulsar vs. Kafka: Architectural Comparison
item.description: How Pulsar separates stateless brokers from BookKeeper storage, how that differs from Kafka's broker-owned logs, and what each costs to operate.

item.title: Kafka Architecture: Topic, Partition, Consumer Group, Offset
item.description: How Kafka builds replicated, ordered partitions, how the ISR and high watermark decide which acknowledged writes survive, and what offsets mean.

item.title: Message Queue vs. Event Streaming: Differences and Use Cases
item.description: How queues delete messages on acknowledgement while event logs keep an ordered history read by offset, and how that decides ordering, replay and fan-out.

item.title: Synchronous Communication Protocols
item.description: Why a caller waiting on a remote answer inherits the callee's latency and failures, how the protocols compare, and how to read this chapter's seven topics.

item.title: API Versioning Strategies
item.description: What makes an API change breaking, where version identifiers can live and how that affects routing and caching, and how to retire old versions safely.

item.title: WebSocket and Server-Sent Events: Real-Time Communication
item.description: How WebSocket handshakes and framing work, how Server-Sent Events stream and resume, and how to run and drain millions of long-lived connections.

item.title: GraphQL: Query Language and Federation Architecture
item.description: How GraphQL executes client-shaped queries, why resolvers cause N+1 fan-out and how batching fixes it, how to bound query cost, and how federation works.

item.title: gRPC Streaming: Unary, Server-Streaming, Bi-directional
item.description: How gRPC's four call types map onto HTTP/2 streams, how flow control becomes backpressure, and why long-lived streams break retries and balancing.

item.title: gRPC & Protocol Buffers: High-Performance RPC
item.description: How Protocol Buffers encodes messages and stays compatible, how gRPC maps calls onto HTTP/2 with deadlines and cancellation, and how the stack fails.

item.title: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3: Multiplexing, HOL Blocking, and QUIC
item.description: How HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, why head-of-line blocking survives it, and how HTTP/3 over QUIC removes it, at what cost.

item.title: REST: Constraints, Resources, and HTTP Contracts
item.description: What REST constraints buy and cost, how HTTP methods, status codes and cache headers form a contract, and how lost updates and duplicates break it.

item.title: Foundations & The Laws of Physics
item.description: The constraints every distributed system inherits: partial failure, explicit timing and fault assumptions, and no shared clock, and where each is covered.

item.title: Time and Ordering
item.description: Why no two machines share a clock, the three ways to order events anyway (physical, logical, hybrid), what each costs, and how to read this chapter.

item.title: Distributed ID Generation: UUIDv7, Snowflake, ULID
item.description: Where uniqueness comes from in Snowflake, UUIDv7 and ULID, how they handle bursts and backward clocks, how ordering affects indexes, and how they fail.

item.title: Google TrueTime & Spanner: Working with Uncertainty
item.description: How TrueTime turns clock error into a bounded interval, how Spanner's commit wait yields external consistency, what it costs, and what a wrong bound breaks.

item.title: Hybrid Logical Clocks (HLC): Combining Physical and Logical Time
item.description: How hybrid logical clocks keep causality while staying close to wall time, what they enable for MVCC snapshots, and how one bad clock spreads.

item.title: Vector Clocks: Detecting Concurrency
item.description: How vector clocks capture happened-before exactly, how version vectors apply them to replicated data, what the metadata costs, and how they break.

item.title: Lamport Timestamps: Capturing Causality
item.description: How Lamport timestamps never invert a causal pair, how a tie-break yields a total order, how Raft terms and Paxos ballots use it, and how implementations fail.
